American Realism. An artistic movement of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries emphasizing unflinching, honest depiction of American life, urban scenes, working people, and rural landscapes without sentimentality or romantic idealization. Painters like Edward Hopper and Thomas Eakins rejected European academic traditions, instead drawing from observation of everyday American experience and revealing psychological isolation, social inequity, and the human condition in its most unvarnished forms.

American Realism emerged as a reaction against European Romanticism and Academic art, which prioritized idealized beauty and historical or mythological subjects. American Realists insisted on direct observation of contemporary American life. Thomas Eakins, from 1844 to 1916, pioneered the movement, depicting scenes from Philadelphia life with scientific precision. His paintings of rowing, surgery, and portraiture emphasize psychological depth and anatomical accuracy.

Winslow Homer, from 1836 to 1910, painted vivid scenes of American work and leisure, soldiers in camp, hunters and fishermen, maritime labor, capturing the roughness and dignity of rural and outdoor life. Edward Hopper, from 1882 to 1967, epitomized twentieth-century American Realism, painting urban isolation through stark compositions of empty diners, gas stations, and hotel rooms. His work conveys psychological alienation in modern American life.

The movement's urban realism focused on gritty city subjects, tenements, factories, and street life rather than picturesque rural scenes. Artists like Robert Henri documented immigrant neighborhoods and working-class communities. American Realism shares characteristics with Naturalism in literature, reflecting a broader cultural commitment to honest social documentation. The movement rejected technical virtuosity for virtuosity's sake, instead valuing truthfulness and emotional honesty. Paintings were often described as ugly by critics accustomed to polished Academic standards.
